units.translation: but, however, indeed. This particle, like the stronger particle ἀλλά [but], which we discussed above on p. 19, has a double force: one adversative, by which the following sentence is opposed to the preceding one, whether negative or affirmative; the other by which a transition is made from one sentence to another (whence it is counted among the conjunctions that make a transition, by Apollonius in his Syntax p. 128, 10 (123, 5 Bekk.) and is called a transitional conjunction by the scholiast on Dionysius Thrax p. 958, 15), when one or more sentences are introduced in succession by δέ [but/and], not so much for the sake of opposition as for continuing and connecting the discourse, as in Latin autem, and indeed in such a way that something is added to what precedes for the sake of explaining, confirming, or giving a reason; in such passages, since καί [and] and γάρ [for] are often no less suitable, many interpreters once believed that δέ [but/and] was often used in place of these particles in passages such as
1. δέ [but/and] in response, where the preceding words of another person are continued,
2. δέ [but/and] placed in a question, although it is placed no differently than in sentences connected to each other outside of a question, nevertheless we add some examples.
4. δέ [but/and] repeated after a word that had preceded (in such passages μέν [on the one hand] is more frequently added in the earlier part of the sentence, as will be shown under the entry μέν)
5. δέ [but/and] is rarer in the apodosis after a conditional sentence, about which I have spoken in the Lexicon Sophocleum p. 108. The examples in Aeschylus are

6. In sentences opposed to each other by μέν [on the one hand] and δέ [but/and], the same or similar words are often repeated. Furthermore, μέν [on the one hand] and δέ [but/and] often correspond to each other after long intervals. Finally, in dialogues the particle μέν [on the one hand], which the first speaker had used, is not infrequently answered by δέ [but/and] in the words of the other speaker. Examples of all these are given under the entry μέν. Since this close connection of sentences by μέν [on the one hand] and δέ [but/and] is not necessary, there is no reason why in passages where δέ [but/and] is placed only in the second part of the sentence, μέν [on the one hand] should be said to have been omitted in the first part, although it could have been suitably added, for example

7. The most usual position of the particle δέ [but/and] is after the first word, or after the second, if the first two are closely connected, such as an article or preposition with a noun, pronoun, adjective, or participle.
After the article and adjective or participle
After the personal pronoun following a vocative
After the noun and adjective (or participle), or in reverse order
After the preposition with its noun
